summary.text: Writing the numerator and denominator as \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\), counting pairs divisible by \(p^i\) gives \(v_p(N(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula and \(\sum_{j\le M}j\lfloor M/j\rfloor\le M^2\) show that \(D(m)\mid N(m)\), so \(v_p(a(m))=v_p(N(m))-v_p(D(m))\). For \(m=np+k\) with \(k<p\), every \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\); this preserves the old denominator terms via Legendre’s formula, and each new index \(np<j\le np+k\) has \(\lfloor m/j\rfloor=1\), so contributes no \(p\)-valuation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le r\le m}\gcd(j,r)
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(m)=\prod_{1\le s\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor!\right)^s.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and obtain formulas for the prime-adic valuations of its numerator and denominator. We then show that both of those valuations are constant as the argument ranges from \(np\) through \(np+p-1\).

Throughout, for a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\).

First recall two elementary valuation facts. For every positive integer \(x\),
\[
v_q(x)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid x},
\]
where only finitely many terms are nonzero. Also, Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_q(t!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Again these sums are finite because their terms vanish once \(q^i>t\). Consequently all the rearrangements of sums below are rearrangements of finite sums.

We first compute the valuation of \(N(m)\). Additivity of valuations over products gives
\[
v_q(N(m))
 =\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{r=1}^m v_q(\gcd(j,r)).
\]
For each pair \((j,r)\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid \gcd(j,r)}.
\]
Now \(q^i\mid\gcd(j,r)\) if and only if \(q^i\mid j\) and \(q^i\mid r\). Therefore, after interchanging the finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{r=1}^m
   \mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid r}\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{r=1}^m\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid r}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The number of multiples of \(q^i\) in \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
 v_q(N(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
}
\tag{1}
\]

Next compute the valuation of the denominator. Additivity of valuations and Legendre's formula give
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{s=1}^m s\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{s=1}^m s\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/s\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
For positive integers \(s,d\), successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/s\rfloor}{d}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{sd}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/d\rfloor}{s}\right\rfloor.
\tag{3}
\]
Thus, on putting \(X_i=\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\) and interchanging the finite sums in (2), we obtain
\[
v_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{s=1}^m s\left\lfloor\frac{X_i}{s}\right\rfloor.
\tag{4}
\]

We need the elementary estimate
\[
\sum_{s=1}^m s\left\lfloor\frac Xs\right\rfloor\le X^2
\qquad(0\le X\le m).
\tag{5}
\]
Indeed, if \(s>X\), then \(\lfloor X/s\rfloor=0\). For each \(1\le s\le X\),
\[
s\left\lfloor\frac Xs\right\rfloor\le X.
\]
There are \(X\) such indices, so their total is at most \(X^2\), proving (5). Since every \(X_i=\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\) lies between \(0\) and \(m\), (4), (5), and (1) imply
\[
v_q(D(m))
 \le\sum_{i\ge1}X_i^2
 =v_q(N(m)).
\tag{6}
\]
This holds for every prime \(q\). Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive: factorials are positive, and all the gcds in the defining product have positive arguments. By unique prime factorization, the inequalities (6) for all primes imply
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\]
For \(m=0\), both empty products are \(1\), so the same conclusion also holds. Thus \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is always an integer. Moreover,
\[
N(m)=D(m)a(m),
\]
and therefore for every prime \(q\),
\[
\boxed{
 v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m)).
}
\tag{7}
\]
The subtraction is legitimate because of (6).

We now fix a positive integer \(n\), a prime \(p\), and an integer \(k\) satisfying
\[
0\le k<p.
\]
Set
\[
M_0=np,\qquad M=np+k.
\]
We will prove separately that
\[
v_p(N(M_0))=v_p(N(M))
\tag{8}
\]
and
\[
v_p(D(M_0))=v_p(D(M)).
\tag{9}
\]

The basic floor identity responsible for both equalities is
\[
\boxed{
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\quad\text{for every }i\ge1.
}
\tag{10}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i\ge1\), division by \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) can be performed by first dividing by \(p\) and then by \(p^{i-1}\). The two first quotients are both \(n\), proving (10).

Applying formula (1) with \(q=p\), and using (10) term by term, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(M))
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =v_p(N(M_0)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (8).

It remains to establish the corresponding equality for the denominator. From its definition,
\[
v_p(D(M))
 =\sum_{s=1}^{M}s\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Ms\right\rfloor!\right).
\tag{11}
\]
We split this sum into the old indices \(1\le s\le np\) and the new indices \(np<s\le np+k\).

First let \(1\le s\le np\). Legendre's formula and the commutation of integer divisions in (3) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor (np+k)/s\rfloor}{p^i}
  \right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor (np+k)/p^i\rfloor}{s}
  \right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (10), this equals
\[
\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor}{s}
  \right\rfloor.
\]
Applying (3) and Legendre's formula in reverse gives
\[
\boxed{
 v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)
 =v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)
}
\quad(1\le s\le np).
\tag{12}
\]
Thus every old index contributes exactly the same amount to the two denominator valuations.

Now consider a new index satisfying
\[
np<s\le np+k.
\tag{13}
\]
We claim that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{s}\right\rfloor=1.
\tag{14}
\]
The upper inequality in (13) gives \(s\le np+k\), so the quotient is at least \(1\). To show it is less than \(2\), use \(k<p\) to get
\[
np+k<(n+1)p.
\]
Since \(n\ge1\), one has \(n+1\le2n\), and therefore
\[
np+k<(n+1)p\le2np<2s,
\]
the last inequality following from \(s>np\). Thus
\(s\le np+k<2s\), which proves (14). It follows that the factorial occurring at every new index is \(1!\), whose \(p\)-adic valuation is zero. Hence all the new terms in (11) vanish:
\[
s\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)
=s\,v_p(1!)=0
\qquad(np<s\le np+k).
\tag{15}
\]
When \(k=0\), there are simply no new indices, and the same conclusion holds.

Combining (11), (12), and (15), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(np+k))
&=\sum_{s=1}^{np+k}s\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{s=1}^{np}s\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np}{s}\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=v_p(D(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (9).

Finally apply the quotient valuation formula (7) at \(m=np\) and at \(m=np+k\). Using (8) and (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np+k))
&=v_p(N(np+k))-v_p(D(np+k))\\
&=v_p(N(np))-v_p(D(np))\\
&=v_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\). Consequently
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
=\cdots=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as claimed.
